title: Economic evaluation of the BabblePlay app intervention to support early vocalising in infants with Down syndrome
official: Economic evaluation of the BabblePlay app intervention to support early vocalising in infants with Down syndrome: a cost-utility analysis alongside a randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Infants with Down syndrome often experience delays in speech and language development. BabblePlay is an app designed to encourage these infants to make more sounds (vocalise) by responding with colourful shapes on a screen when they speak. While the main BabblePlay trial (https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN12366576) is testing whether the app improves language skills, it is also important to know if it is a good use of limited healthcare budgets. Hence, this study is an "economic evaluation" running alongside that main trial. The study goal is to determine if BabblePlay provides "value for money" for the NHS and social services compared to the usual care families receive. It will look at whether the costs of the intervention are justified by improvements in the children’s health-related quality of life.

Who can participate?
Participants are families already enrolled in the BabblePlay clinical trial (ISRCTN12366576). These are UK-based families with an infant (aged 7–15 months) who has a diagnosis of Down syndrome and lives in a monolingual English-speaking household, has eyesight good enough to see shapes on a screen, and is not enrolled in another speech, language or communication intervention study. 

What does the study involve?
This research is all done remotely. Caregivers will be asked to complete online questionnaires (including both tailored resource use and quality of life questionnaires) at two time points: at the start (baseline) and 11 months after the initial activity period.
- Tailored resource use questionnaire: Caregivers will report on their child’s use of health and social care services (such as speech therapy or GP visits) to help us calculate total costs.
- Quality of Life (QoL) questionnaires: Caregivers will complete two specific surveys (the IQI designed for infants under 1 year and the EQ-TIPS designed for children aged 1–3) to measure their child’s wellbeing and development.
By combining information on costs and quality of life, we can determine the "cost-effectiveness" of the app.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Possible benefits: There are no direct clinical benefits to participating in this specific economic sub-study. However, the results will help the NHS and policymakers decide whether to fund and provide BabblePlay to other families in the UK.

Possible risks: There are no physical risks. The only "burden" is the small amount of extra time required for caregivers to complete the online questionnaires.

Where is the study run from?
The University of York, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
February 2026 to December 2026.

Who is funding the study? 
The University of York, UK.

Who is the main contact?
Prof Tamar Keren-Portnoy, tamar.keren-portnoy@york.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Same as the BabblePlay RCT:
1. The infant has a diagnosis of Down syndrome
2. The infant is aged between 7 and 15 months at the point of randomisation
3. The infant is growing up in a monolingual English-speaking household, or is exposed to less than 10% of another language, based on caregiver report
4. The infant has eyesight good enough to view shapes on an iPad screen (based on caregiver report)
5. Twins (triplets/quadruplets/….) are eligible to participate
6. The family is based in the UK
7. The infant is not taking part in another speech, language or communication intervention research study
Exclusion criteria:
Same as the BabblePlay RCT:
1. Infant does not meet the diagnosis, age, language exposure, or residency requirements listed above
2. Infant has visual difficulties that would prevent them from seeing shapes on the iPad screen
3. Infant is currently in another speech, language, or communication intervention research study
